marketable-limit-order-satisfiable-by-cu.text: A marketable limit order has a limit price already satisfiable by the current order book, such as a buy limit at $90 when the ask is $86.41.

mars1-first-computerized-reservation-195.text: MARS-1 (1958), built by Hitachi for Japanese National Railways, was the world's first computerized seat reservation system (for trains, not airlines).

maryland-hb0895-grocery-personal-data-pr.text: Maryland HB0895 (signed April 2026, effective October 2026) bans grocery stores from using personal data to raise prices, with $10K first offense and $25K repeat penalties.

master-copy-principle-transcode-from-los.text: Best practice is to retain a lossless or uncompressed master copy and always transcode from the master, never from a previously transcoded copy, to avoid cumulative quality loss

master-worker-bottleneck-fix-shared-queu.text: In master-worker load balancing, the master is a single point of contention; the fix is replacing the master with a shared task queue, not adding more masters

matrix-clock-diagonal-own-logical-clock.text: In a matrix clock, the diagonal entry [i][i] corresponds to host i's own logical clock, equivalent to its vector clock entry.

matrix-clock-entry-interpretation.text: In a matrix clock, entry [i][j] of the N×N matrix represents host i's knowledge of host j's logical time.

matrix-clock-generalizes-vector-clocks.text: Matrix clocks generalize vector clocks: a vector clock is a single row, and a matrix clock is the full set of rows across all hosts.

matrix-clock-global-lower-bound.text: In a matrix clock, min_i(M[i][j]) across all rows gives the guaranteed minimum logical time that all processes have observed for process j, enabling safe garbage collection of obsolete data.

matrix-clock-knows-what-others-know.text: Matrix clocks let a process determine what other processes know about system state, not just what it knows itself — enabling distributed checkpointing and garbage collection.

matrix-clock-message-includes-full-matri.text: When a message is sent in a matrix clock system, the sender includes its entire matrix — not just its own vector clock — so the receiver learns what the sender knows about all other hosts.

matrix-clock-n-squared-overhead.text: Matrix clocks are N×N matrices (for N processes) with O(N²) space and communication overhead, compared to O(N) for vector clocks.

max-min-heap-analogue-root-max-min-child.text: A max-min heap is the analogue of a min-max heap with the maximum at the root and the minimum at a child of the root.

mcconnell-code-complete-defines-fan-out-.text: McConnell's Code Complete defines fan-out in the context of design construction as a key consideration for managing complexity.

md5-sha1-broken-for-collisions.text: MD5 and SHA-1 both have demonstrated collision attacks and are not suitable for security-critical applications

md5-sha1-collision-resistance-broken.text: MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collision attacks and should not be used for security-critical applications; SHA-2, SHA-3, and BLAKE2/BLAKE3 remain collision-resistant.

memory-hierarchy-sram-dram-flash-disk.text: The memory technology hierarchy from fastest/most expensive to slowest/cheapest is: SRAM > DRAM > Flash > Hard Disk.

mergeable-sketches-complete-stream-analy.text: The algebraic mergeability of probabilistic sketches (Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch) supports coordination-free distributed combination of partial results, and the complementary tradeoffs between Count-Min Sketch (biased, never undercounts) and Count Sketch (unbiased, may undercount) provide flexibility in choosing frequency estimation strategies for distributed stream analytics.

justifications.label: Mergeability enables distributed deployment; complementary estimators cover both biased-safe and unbiased-accurate use cases

merkle-root-guarantees-data-integrity.text: A Merkle tree root hash cryptographically commits to all underlying data, providing tamper-evident verification with O(log n) proof size.

justifications.label: Without domain separation between leaf and internal hashes, an attacker can construct a different tree with the same root — the commitment guarantee requires the defense to be in place

merkle-tree-anti-entropy-cassandra-riak.text: Cassandra and Riak use Merkle trees in their anti-entropy protocols to efficiently identify out-of-sync key ranges between replicas, minimizing unnecessary data transfer

merkle-tree-arbitrary-branching-factors.text: Merkle trees can use arbitrary branching factors, though most implementations are binary.

merkle-tree-blockchain-spv.text: Bitcoin and Ethereum use Merkle trees to structure transactions within blocks, enabling simplified payment verification (SPV) of individual transactions without downloading the full block

merkle-tree-cryptographic-hash-sha2-crc-.text: Merkle trees typically use a cryptographic hash such as SHA-2 for tamper resistance, while CRCs suffice when protecting only against accidental corruption.

merkle-tree-generalizes-hash-lists-and-h.text: A Merkle tree generalizes both hash lists and hash chains.

merkle-tree-incremental-branch-verificat.text: Merkle tree branches can be verified independently without having the full tree, enabling parallel downloading and immediate integrity checking of individual data blocks

merkle-tree-invented-1979-ralph-merkle.text: Merkle trees were invented by Ralph Merkle and patented in 1979 (US Patent 4,309,569)

merkle-tree-leaf-verification-log-n.text: Verifying that a leaf belongs to a Merkle tree requires O(log n) hashes (a Merkle proof), compared to O(n) for a hash list

merkle-tree-root-hash-commits-to-all-dat.text: The root hash of a Merkle tree acts as a cryptographic commitment to all underlying data, and must be obtained from a trusted source before verification

merkle-tree-second-preimage-attack-domai.text: Merkle trees are vulnerable to second preimage attacks because the root hash does not encode tree depth; Certificate Transparency mitigates this by prepending 0x00 to leaf hash inputs and 0x01 to internal node hash inputs

merkle-tree-structure-leaf-and-internal-.text: A Merkle tree leaf node contains the cryptographic hash of a data block, and each internal node contains the hash of its children's concatenated hashes.

merkle-trees-universal-distributed-integ.text: Merkle trees provide the shared O(log n) integrity verification foundation for both distributed database anti-entropy (Cassandra, Dynamo) and blockchain simplified payment verification, using the same structure for fundamentally different trust models.

justifications.label: Log-n verification cost makes Merkle trees the default integrity primitive whether the adversary is network delay (databases) or Byzantine peers (blockchain)

message-delivery-guarantees-three-types.text: Distributed systems commonly distinguish three delivery guarantees: at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once.

message-queue-and-pub-sub-sibling-patter.text: Message queues and publish/subscribe are related but distinct patterns, and most middleware systems such as JMS support both.

message-queue-async-temporal-decoupling.text: Message queues implement asynchronous communication where producers and consumers are temporally decoupled — sender and receiver do not need to be active at the same time

message-queue-competing-consumers-patter.text: The Competing Consumers pattern allows multiple concurrent consumers to process messages from the same queue, enabling horizontal scaling and parallel processing

message-queue-durability-spectrum.text: Message queue durability trades off reliability against performance across a spectrum: in-memory (fastest, least reliable) < disk < DBMS-backed (slowest, most reliable)

message-queue-protocols-amqp-stomp-mqtt.text: Three key open message queuing standards are AMQP (feature-rich, ISO/IEC 19464, application layer), STOMP (text-oriented, simple, application layer), and MQTT (lightweight, designed for IoT/embedded, transport layer)

message-queue-scope-os-internal-vs-cross.text: Message queues can be internal to an OS or application (SYS V, POSIX queues) or span multiple systems (IBM MQ, RabbitMQ, SQS).

messaging-architecture-decomposes-along-.text: Messaging systems exhibit two recurring architectural separations — routing from content (observed in email's envelope vs headers and EDA's broker topology vs payload design) and producers from consumers in time (observed across store-and-forward systems from email to Kafka) — though the antecedents establish each separation independently and do not directly demonstrate that the routing-content separation holds at every point on the temporal decoupling spectrum.

justifications.label: Two independently derived messaging invariants (structural separation and temporal decoupling) are orthogonal dimensions of the same design space

messaging-converges-on-routing-content-s.text: Messaging architectures at all scales converge on separating routing concerns from content concerns — email's SMTP envelope vs RFC 5322 headers and EDA's broker/mediator topology vs fat/thin payload design are independent instantiations of the same architectural decomposition, suggesting routing-content separation is a structural invariant of message-passing systems.

justifications.label: Two independent messaging paradigms (email 1971, EDA modern) both decompose into routing/transport vs content/semantics layers

messaging-decomposition-grounded-in-dist.text: Messaging architecture's two orthogonal decompositions — routing/content separation and temporal/spatial decoupling — appear to have natural correspondences with the distributed data plane's dual primitives: temporal decoupling relies on sequential persistence (the durability primitive) while routing decisions benefit from distributed topology awareness served by partitioning (the distribution primitive), suggesting that abstract messaging properties map onto concrete infrastructure requirements.

justifications.label: The messaging decomposition axes and the distributed data primitives map onto each other — temporal decoupling maps to persistence and routing maps to partitioning — revealing that messaging abstractions are not free-floating but depend on specific infrastructure capabilities

meta-architecture-concretizes-dual-unive.text: The complete distributed meta-architecture (persistence + distribution-compensation) aligns with the two orthogonal dimensions of architectural universality — immutability relates to the persistence dimension and logarithmic bounds relate to the distribution-compensation dimension — suggesting that the meta-architecture may represent a concrete realization of these universal properties, though the antecedents establish the orthogonality of each pair independently rather than directly proving the mapping between them.

justifications.label: The abstract universals (immutability-depth, logarithmic-breadth) map one-to-one onto the meta-architecture's dimensions (persistence, distribution-compensation)

meta-architecture-persistence-exhibits-d.text: The distributed meta-architecture's persistence dimension exhibits a compound duality — it inherits the append-only principle's universal duality (simultaneously most-validated AND most-constraining) and this duality manifests concretely as two joint architectural consequences (WAL's durability backbone and immutability's plane-collapse), making the persistence dimension simultaneously the most powerful and the most demanding aspect of the meta-architecture.

justifications.label: The abstract validation/constraint duality and its concrete durability/plane-collapse manifestation combine in the persistence dimension

meta-architecture-persistence-inherits-a.text: The distributed meta-architecture's persistence dimension inherits the append-only principle's universal duality — it is simultaneously the most validated and the most constraining dimension, being confirmed across spatial and temporal axes while creating the read-write asymmetry that demands compensation throughout the architecture.

justifications.label: The meta-architecture's persistence half inherits validation-plus-constraint from the append-only principle that defines it

method-injection-passes-dependencies-as-.text: Method injection passes dependencies as method arguments for temporary or per-call use, with no long-term reference held.

microsoft-distributed-query-ole-db.text: A Microsoft distributed query is any SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement referencing tables from one or more external OLE DB data sources.

mid-squares-hashing-extracts-middle-digi.text: Mid-squares hashing squares the key and extracts middle digits to produce the hash value.

min-max-heap-alternating-levels.text: A min-max heap uses alternating min levels (even: 0, 2, 4) and max levels (odd: 1, 3, 5), where every node on a min level is smaller than all its descendants and every node on a max level is greater than all its descendants

min-max-heap-find-min-max-constant-time.text: In a min-max heap, find-min is O(1) (always the root) and find-max is O(1) (always one of the root's two children, requiring at most one comparison)

min-max-heap-implements-depq.text: A min-max heap is a primary implementation strategy for double-ended priority queues (DEPQs), providing constant-time access to both minimum and maximum elements

min-max-heap-insert-delete-log-n-build-l.text: Min-max heap insert and delete operations are O(log n), and the heap can be built in O(n) time using bottom-up Floyd's construction, same as standard binary heaps

min-max-heap-invented-1986.text: The min-max heap was invented in 1986 by Atkinson, Sack, Santoro, and Strothotte.

min-max-heap-level-index-floor-log2.text: In an array-backed min-max heap indexed from 1, the level of the node at index i is floor(log2(i)).

min-max-heap-push-down-checks-six-nodes.text: In a min-max heap, push-down must check both children and grandchildren (up to 6 nodes: 2 children + 4 grandchildren) to find the smallest or largest descendant

min-max-heap-push-up-grandparent-compari.text: In min-max heap push-up, insertion compares with the grandparent two levels up because same-type levels alternate every two levels.

min-max-heap-tail-recursion-o1-space.text: Both push-up and push-down in a min-max heap are tail-recursive and can be implemented iteratively in O(1) space.

min-max-median-heap-supports-order-stati.text: A min-max-median heap is a variant that supports order-statistic operations including find-median, delete-median, find(k), and delete(k).

minimum-feedback-vertex-set-np-hard.text: Finding the minimum feedback vertex set or feedback arc set to make a cyclic graph acyclic is NP-hard.

mixed-graph-directed-undirected.text: A mixed graph contains both directed and undirected edges and is written G = (V, E, A).

mktemp-unsafe-use-mkstemp.text: mktemp() is unsafe because it creates a TOCTOU window; mkstemp() should be used instead as it atomically creates and opens the file

mobile-im-surpassed-sms-2013.text: Mobile instant messaging surpassed SMS in global message volume by 2013, driven by free data-based messaging vs. per-message SMS costs

modula-1975-designed-for-modular-program.text: Modula (1975) by Niklaus Wirth was one of the first languages designed from the start for modular programming.

modular-programming-1968-symposium-larry.text: The term modular programming was used at the 1968 National Symposium on Modular Programming organized by Larry Constantine.

modular-programming-dag-dependencies.text: Module dependencies should form a directed acyclic graph (DAG); cyclic dependencies between modules indicate they should be merged into a single module

modular-programming-high-cohesion-low-co.text: Effective modular design aims for high cohesion (elements within a module belong together) and low coupling (minimal interdependence between modules)

modular-programming-information-hiding-1.text: Information hiding, the principle that a module should conceal its internal workings from other modules, was formalized by David Parnas in 1972

modular-programming-interface-and-implem.text: In modular programming, a module exposes a well-defined interface and contains an implementation behind that interface.

modularity-is-subset-of-soc.text: Modularity is a subset of separation of concerns (separation by size applied to code components); SoC is broader and also applies to project phases, specifications, and analysis perspectives

module-vs-component-scope.text: A module is a piece of an individual program, while a component is a higher-level piece of a whole system.

moldable-vs-malleable-load-balancing-alg.text: Moldable algorithms adapt to varying processor counts but must be fixed before execution; malleable algorithms handle fluctuating processor counts during execution.

mongodb-auto-sharding-since-v1-6.text: MongoDB has supported automatic sharding since version 1.6, using the command sh.shardCollection("db.collection", { "shardKey": 1 }).

monotone-and-antitone-implies-constant.text: A function that is both monotone and antitone on a lattice must be constant

monotone-discontinuities-jump-or-removab.text: Monotone functions can only have jump or removable discontinuities (never oscillatory), and the set of discontinuities is at most countable

monotone-interval-differentiable-almost-.text: A monotone function on an interval is differentiable almost everywhere (Lebesgue's theorem), with the set of non-differentiable points having Lebesgue measure zero

monotone-interval-riemann-integrable.text: A monotone function on a closed interval [a,b] is Riemann integrable with no additional conditions required

monotonic-decreasing-reverses-order.text: A monotonically decreasing function satisfies x ≤ y implies f(x) ≥ f(y), reversing order.

monotonic-heuristic-implies-admissible.text: A monotonic (consistent) heuristic implies admissibility (h(n) ≤ c(n,a,n') + h(n')), but an admissible heuristic is not necessarily monotonic

monotonic-increasing-preserves-order.text: A monotonically increasing function satisfies x ≤ y implies f(x) ≤ f(y), preserving order.

morris-counter-asymptotically-optimal.text: Nelson and Yu (2020) proved that a slight modification to the Morris Counter is asymptotically optimal among all algorithms for the approximate counting problem

morris-counter-computer-implementation-g.text: A computer implementation of the Morris counter generates c pseudo-random bits, computes their logical AND, and adds the result to the counter on each increment request.

morris-counter-custom-value-sets-tradeof.text: Custom counter value sets in approximate counting can be optimized for desired error ratio, memory budget, or counting range.

morris-counter-increment-4-to-8-probabil.text: When the Morris counter estimate is 4, an increment request moves it to 8 with probability 1/4 and leaves it at 4 with probability 3/4.

morris-counter-precursor-streaming-algor.text: The approximate counting algorithm (Morris 1977, analyzed by Flajolet 1980s) is considered a direct precursor to modern streaming algorithms; the problem of frequency moments in data streams grew from this work

morris-counter-probabilistic-increment.text: The Morris Counter increments with probability 2^(-c) where c is the current stored value; the resulting estimator is mathematically unbiased

morris-counter-smaller-values-greater-er.text: In the Morris approximate counting algorithm, smaller counter values have greater error ratios than larger values.

morris-counter-stores-exponent-only.text: The Morris approximate counting algorithm stores only the exponent, not the count itself — estimated count is 2^c where c is the stored value, requiring O(log log n) memory to count up to n events

most-commercial-recommenders-are-hybrid.text: Most commercial recommender systems are hybrid, combining memory-based and model-based collaborative filtering approaches to overcome sparsity and information loss

most-search-engines-use-proximity-as-imp.text: Most commercial search engines use proximity as an implicit ranking signal rather than exposing explicit proximity operators in query syntax

mu-puzzle-invariant-impossibility-proof-.text: The MU Puzzle invariant proof technique establishes initial truth, shows preservation under all transformation rules, then concludes unreachability of target states that violate the invariant

multi-keyword-proximity-specifies-which-.text: With three or more keywords, multi-keyword proximity search requires specifying which subsets of keywords should be proximate.

multi-master-replication-on3-degradation.text: Jim Gray's analysis shows multi-master replication under a transactional model degrades as O(n³) unless data has a natural partition key

multi-model-databases-support-multiple-d.text: Multi-model NoSQL databases such as ArangoDB, Cosmos DB, and MarkLogic support multiple data models in a single engine.

multiple-data-structures-implement-same-.text: Multiple concrete data structures can implement the same ADT (e.g., array-based list vs. linked list both implement the list ADT)

mutex-four-process-states-cycle.text: Mutual exclusion processes cycle through Non-Critical Section, Trying, Critical Section, and Exit.

mutex-lockout-lower-bound-sqrt-n-states.text: Avoiding lockout in mutual exclusion requires Ω(√n) distinct memory states; avoiding unbounded waiting requires n states

mutex-ownership-semaphore-no-ownership.text: A mutex has ownership semantics — only the thread that acquired it should release it; a semaphore does not have this ownership constraint and any thread can release it

mutex-two-correctness-properties.text: The two minimum correctness properties for mutual exclusion are: (1) mutual exclusion — only one process in the critical section at a time, and (2) deadlock freedom — some waiting process must eventually enter

mutual-exclusion-prevents-race-condition.text: Mutual exclusion prevents race conditions by ensuring only one thread of execution can access a critical section at a time.

mvcc-readers-get-prior-version.text: Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC) serves readers the prior unmodified version of data being changed by another transaction, so writers don't block readers and vice versa

mysql-myisam-no-transactions-innodb-yes.text: MySQL's MyISAM storage engine does not support transactions; InnoDB (default since MySQL 5.5) does

mysql-postgres-use-btree-not-bplus.text: MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Firebird use regular B-trees, not B+ trees; SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle, and IBM Db2 use B+ trees

napster-centralized-index-single-point-f.text: Napster used a centralized index that created a single point of failure, in contrast to DHT structured routing.

navitaire-new-skies-powers-low-cost-carr.text: Navitaire's New Skies powers low-cost carriers including Ryanair, IndiGo, AirAsia, Wizz Air, Spirit, and Frontier.

nc-polylogarithmic-time-polynomial-proce.text: The NC complexity class captures problems solvable in polylogarithmic time with polynomial processors and is equivalent under PRAM and Boolean circuit models.

negative-cycles-make-shortest-path-undef.text: Negative cycles make shortest paths undefined because a path can loop infinitely for a lower cost.

nested-transactions-contain-subtransacti.text: Nested transactions contain statements that start sub-transactions.

network-partition-division-into-independ.text: A network partition is a division of a computer network into relatively independent subnets.

network-partition-nodes-still-function.text: A network partition means nodes cannot communicate across the partition boundary, but nodes within each partition continue operating normally

new-york-algorithmic-pricing-disclosure-.text: New York's Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act (November 2025) requires disclosure when personal data sets prices and provides up to $1,000 per violation.

nfc-used-for-contactless-wallet-transact.text: NFC (Near Field Communication) is the wireless protocol used to pass credentials from a digital wallet to a merchant terminal for contactless transactions

nist-csf-2-five-functions.text: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 structures security measures across five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover

nist-sp-800-53-twenty-control-families.text: NIST SP 800-53 organizes security controls into 20 families across management, operational, and technical domains

nist-sp800-131a-minimum-112bit-security-.text: NIST SP 800-131A (2011) required minimum 112-bit security (SHA-2) for federal use starting 2014, replacing the 80-bit level provided by SHA-1

non-admissible-heuristic-causes-suboptim.text: If a heuristic overestimates, A* may skip the optimal path because f(n) appears too expensive, leading to suboptimal solutions.

non-recursive-locks-single-entry-reentry.text: Non-recursive locks allow a single entry; re-entry by the same thread causes deadlock or exception.

non-refundable-tickets-alternative-to-ov.text: Non-refundable tickets are an alternative to overbooking that discourages no-shows by making cancellation costly, common with low-cost carriers.

non-relational-databases-date-to-late-19.text: Non-relational databases date back to the late 1960s.

nosql-ap-default-aligns-with-cap-product.text: NoSQL databases' default AP preference aligns with the CAP theorem's production lineage split — most NoSQL systems occupy the same design space as Dynamo/Cassandra, inheriting leaderless replication and eventual consistency as architectural defaults.

justifications.label: NoSQL's AP default is not arbitrary — it reflects the same CAP bifurcation that produced the Dynamo/Cassandra production lineage

nosql-ap-lineage-inherits-complete-conve.text: NoSQL databases' default AP preference inherits the full AP convergence mechanism — not just leaderless replication topology but the complete three-layer convergence stack (gossip for dissemination, Merkle anti-entropy for divergence detection, vector clocks for causality) established by the Dynamo production lineage.

justifications.label: NoSQL's AP default implies inheritance of the complete convergence mechanism, not merely the replication topology

nosql-denormalization-reads-exceed-write.text: Denormalization in NoSQL (embedding foreign values) avoids lookups but requires updating multiple locations when source data changes, making it best suited when reads far exceed writes

nosql-emerged-early-2000s-web2-scalabili.text: The NoSQL term emerged in the early 2000s driven by Web 2.0 scalability needs.

nosql-four-primary-data-models.text: NoSQL databases use four primary data models: key-value, document, wide-column, and graph, each optimized for different access patterns

nosql-key-value-highest-perf-lowest-inte.text: Key-value stores offer the highest performance and scalability with the simplest data model but lowest data integrity guarantees among NoSQL types

nosql-means-not-only-sql.text: NoSQL means 'Not Only SQL' and can coexist with SQL databases in polyglot-persistent architectures.

nosql-most-prioritize-ap-over-c.text: Most NoSQL systems prioritize availability and partition tolerance (AP) over strict consistency in the CAP theorem tradeoff, using eventual consistency where updates propagate to all nodes eventually

nosql-non-indexed-field-full-scan.text: Querying non-indexed fields in most NoSQL systems causes full collection or table scans

nosql-performance-measured-by-throughput.text: NoSQL performance is often measured by throughput in operations per second using benchmarks such as YCSB.

nosql-scales-horizontally-across-commodi.text: NoSQL databases are designed to scale horizontally across clusters of commodity machines.

nosql-systems-use-wal-to-prevent-lost-wr.text: Some NoSQL systems use write-ahead logging (WAL) to prevent data loss from lost writes.

nosql-three-relational-data-techniques.text: Three techniques for handling relational data in NoSQL: (1) multiple queries, (2) denormalization/caching foreign values, (3) nesting data within documents

notable-tsdb-implementation-languages.text: Notable open-source TSDBs and their implementation languages include InfluxDB (Go/Rust), Prometheus (Go), TimescaleDB (C, PostgreSQL extension), VictoriaMetrics (Go), ClickHouse (C++), and Apache IoTDB (Java).

notification-emns-emergency-mass-notific.text: Emergency Mass Notification Services (EMNS) are notification services specifically used for emergency alerting such as evacuation warnings and facility closures

notification-enterprise-sqlserver-blackb.text: SQL Server Notification Services and Blackboard Connect are domain-specific notification implementations for database events and education respectively.

notification-fan-out-one-to-many-core.text: The core architectural concern of notification services is one-to-many message delivery (fan-out).

notification-non-emergency-flight-status.text: Non-emergency notification services can send airline flight status updates to passengers via cellphone.

notification-personalized-vs-broadcast.text: Notification messages can be identical broadcasts to all recipients or personalized per recipient, where personalization requires per-recipient rendering and increases system complexity

notification-platform-push-services.text: Major platform-specific push notification services are APNs (Apple), FCM (Google, successor to GCM), WNS (Windows), and Amazon SNS (AWS managed pub/sub)

notification-self-hosted-vs-managed.text: Notification infrastructure can be self-hosted (sender-owned) or provided as a managed service (service-provider-owned), representing a key architectural decision

notification-service-multi-channel-deliv.text: A notification service broadcasts messages to many recipients simultaneously across multiple channels including email, telephone, fax, and text messages

notification-vs-message-queuing-fanout-f.text: Notification services relate to message queuing because both deal with asynchronous message delivery, but notification services focus on fan-out to end users rather than inter-service communication.

ntfs-append-data-not-true-immutability.text: NTFS has a 'Create Folders / Append Data' ACL permission but it does not enforce true immutability of existing data

ntp-accuracy-milliseconds-udp.text: NTP achieves few-millisecond accuracy over the public Internet and sub-millisecond over LANs, using UDP as its transport protocol

nullipotent-operation-no-side-effects.text: A nullipotent operation has no side effects at all; HTTP GET is given as an example.

nvod-staggered-broadcast-10-20-min.text: Near Video on Demand (NVOD) staggers the same content across multiple channels at 10–20 minute intervals as a broadcast-era approximation of true VOD, primarily used by satellite providers lacking a broadband return path

object-freeze-shallow-immutability-javas.text: JavaScript's Object.freeze(obj) provides shallow immutability for an object.

object-storage-cloud-implementations.text: Major cloud object storage implementations include Amazon S3 (launched 2006), Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage (launched 2010), and OpenStack Swift

object-storage-complements-not-replaces-.text: Object storage complements but does not replace NAS (no file-level locking) or SAN (no block-level access).

object-storage-eventual-consistency.text: Object stores typically offer eventual consistency, while key-value stores offer strong consistency; object stores also add per-object metadata and handle larger data sizes (hundreds of MB+)

object-storage-flat-namespace.text: Object storage uses a flat namespace where objects are addressed by unique IDs within buckets, eliminating hierarchical path dependencies and name collisions

object-storage-lustre-supercomputers.text: Lustre, an object-based file system, runs on approximately 70% of the Top 100 supercomputers and contacts metadata servers only at file open, then communicates directly with object storage servers

object-storage-not-for-transactional-dat.text: Object storage is not suitable for transactional workloads because it lacks file-level locking and sharing mechanisms required for concurrent updates

object-storage-objects-no-fixed-size.text: Objects in object storage have no fixed size; partitions and objects grow dynamically subject only to physical or quota limits.

object-storage-optimized-for-write-once-.text: Object storage's flat namespace, lack of POSIX locking, and eventual consistency model converge on a write-once-read-many (WORM) architectural sweet spot — optimized for immutable blob storage with metadata-enriched retrieval, fundamentally unsuited for transactional or mutable-state workloads.

justifications.label: Three design choices independently point toward immutable blob storage as the optimal use case

object-storage-osd-v1-addressing.text: OSD v1 uses 64-bit partition ID + 64-bit object ID for addressing; OSD v2 added snapshots (read-only via copy-on-write), clones (writable copies), and collections

object-storage-per-object-and-per-comman.text: Object storage supports per-object and per-command access control at the device level.

object-storage-separates-metadata-and-da.text: Object storage separates metadata operations from data operations to optimize performance and scale them independently.

object-storage-three-components.text: Each object in object storage consists of three parts: data (arbitrary bytes), metadata (extensible key-value attributes), and a globally unique identifier

occ-aka-optimistic-locking-non-locking.text: OCC is also called optimistic locking despite being a non-locking technique; the name refers to the optimistic assumption, not the mechanism.

occ-can-be-implemented-on-mvcc.text: OCC can be implemented on top of Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC), a related technique used by Firebird and PostgreSQL.

occ-four-phases.text: Optimistic concurrency control has four phases executed in order: Begin (record timestamp), Modify (tentative writes), Validate (check for conflicts), Commit/Rollback (finalize or abort)

occ-hidden-form-field-web-pattern.text: In web applications, a hidden form field storing original content, timestamp, or sequence number can be compared on submit to detect OCC conflicts.

occ-http-etag-mechanism.text: HTTP's ETag header combined with If-Match on PUT requests implements OCC natively in the HTTP protocol: the server rejects a PUT if the ETag is stale

occ-low-contention-advantage.text: OCC performs well under low contention where conflicts are rare; under high contention, repeated transaction restarts degrade performance compared to pessimistic locking

occ-mirrors-optimistic-replication-at-di.text: Optimistic concurrency control and optimistic replication are the same validate-then-commit pattern operating at different scales — OCC validates within a single database before commit, while optimistic replication validates across replicas at merge time, both accepting concurrent reads/writes and detecting conflicts retroactively.

justifications.label: OCC and optimistic replication share the same structure: allow concurrent access, detect conflicts at commit/merge time, reject on violation

occ-proposed-1979-kung-robinson.text: Optimistic concurrency control was first proposed by H.T. Kung and John T. Robinson in 1979.

occ-stateless-protocols-favor-occ.text: Stateless protocols like HTTP favor OCC over pessimistic locking because holding locks across user interactions is impractical since users may abandon sessions without releasing locks

occ-systems-implementations.text: Systems implementing OCC include Kubernetes (resourceVersion), DynamoDB (conditional writes), Elasticsearch (sequence numbers), Redis (WATCH command), and CouchDB (document revisions)

occ-validate-commit-must-be-atomic.text: The validate and commit phases of OCC must be performed atomically to prevent time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerabilities

occ-validation-checks-read-write-conflic.text: The OCC validate phase checks whether other transactions committed after this one started, or still active, modified data this transaction read or wrote.

oco-order-one-cancels-other.text: In a One Cancels Other (OCO) order pair, when one leg executes, the other is automatically canceled.

oco-vs-oso-orders.text: OCO (one-cancels-other) cancels one order when the other executes; OSO (one-sends-other) submits a secondary order when the primary executes — they are directionally opposite

one-time-mac-pairwise-independent-hash-f.text: A one-time MAC based on a pairwise independent hash can use the formula tag = (a*m + b) mod p, with key (a,b) and p prime.

open-addressing-is-closed-hashing.text: Open addressing is also called closed hashing, and separate chaining is also called open hashing — the terminology is inverted.

open-addressing-load-factor-threshold.text: For open addressing, the recommended maximum load factor is 0.6–0.75; for separate chaining, optimal load factor range is 1–3.

open-addressing-slot-holds-at-most-one-i.text: Open addressing stores at most one item per slot and resolves a collision by probing for the next empty slot.

open-addressing-slot-states.text: Open addressing requires tracking three slot states (occupied, empty, deleted) because removing an item can break probe chains.

open-addressing-three-probing-methods.text: The three standard probing methods for open addressing are linear probing, quadratic probing, and double hashing.

opml-imports-exports-feed-subscription-l.text: OPML (Outline Processor Markup Language) is used for importing/exporting feed subscription lists between aggregators.

optimal-revisit-policy-penalizes-frequen.text: The optimal re-visit policy penalizes pages that change too often — it is neither uniform nor proportional, but closer to uniform.

optimistic-duality-safe-across-scales-un.text: The optimistic validate-then-commit pattern's scale-invariance — operating identically from single-node OCC (validate at commit, advantage under low contention) through CAP-driven AP replication (optimistic replication with eventual consistency) — achieves safe concurrent operation at all scales unless validity constraint hazards break the invariance: concurrent updates that individually satisfy local invariants can collectively violate global constraints, a failure mode that single-node OCC catches at validation time but distributed optimistic replication cannot detect without cross-node coordination.

justifications.label: Scale-invariant optimistic duality breaks when global validity constraints require coordination that optimistic replication foregoes

optimistic-replication-coda-disconnected.text: The Coda distributed file system applies optimistic replication for disconnected operation.

optimistic-replication-crdts-avoid-expli.text: CRDTs avoid conflicts by design, eliminating the need for explicit conflict resolution.

optimistic-replication-cvs-five-element-.text: CVS illustrates the five optimistic replication elements: local file edits as submission, manual push/pull propagation, arrival order at central server as schedule, manual conflict fixes as resolution, and central server acceptance as commitment.

optimistic-replication-eventual-consiste.text: Optimistic replication allows replicas to diverge temporarily, guaranteeing only eventual consistency: replicas converge once the system quiesces, trading strict consistency for availability and concurrency

optimistic-replication-five-elements.text: Optimistic replication has five algorithmic elements: operation submission, propagation, scheduling, conflict resolution, and commitment

optimistic-replication-non-idempotent-da.text: Non-idempotent operations (e.g., increment) under replication lag are dangerous because users may retry operations that appeared to fail, causing duplicate side effects

optimistic-replication-pessimistic-ident.text: Pessimistic replication enforces that all replicas are identical at all times, as if there were a single copy.

optimistic-replication-requires-idempote.text: Optimistic replication's allowance of concurrent updates creates a structural danger from non-idempotent operations — retries during replication lag can cause duplicate side effects, making idempotency the safety net that prevents the optimistic model from producing corrupted state.

justifications.label: Optimistic replication enables concurrent mutations; idempotency prevents the duplicate application of retried operations from corrupting state

optimistic-replication-state-vs-operatio.text: Replication propagation uses either state transfer (send current state) or operation transfer (send operations to reach new state); state transfer cannot use semantic conflict resolution because it lacks operation-level information

optimistic-replication-sync-special-case.text: Synchronization is a special case of replication with exactly two replicas (e.g., PDA syncing with a computer); replication is the broader problem

optimistic-replication-syntactic-vs-sema.text: Optimistic replication scheduling and conflict resolution can be syntactic (using general metadata such as timestamps or origin) or semantic (using application-specific knowledge).

optimistic-replication-usenet-thomas-wri.text: Usenet and similar systems use the Thomas Write Rule for conflict resolution.

optimistic-replication-validity-constrai.text: Two individually valid updates can be mutually incompatible when combined; the system must detect this at merge time, pick a winner, and roll back the loser across all nodes

optimization-cascades-through-algorithm-.text: Data structure optimization cascades multiplicatively through algorithm inheritance chains — the heap optimization spectrum (binary → binomial → Fibonacci, with each successor improving amortized complexity) propagates through the shortest-path inheritance chain (Bellman-Ford → Dijkstra → A*/Yen's), meaning each improvement in the underlying priority queue automatically improves all algorithms that inherit it as a subroutine, creating a compounding effect where structure-level and algorithm-level optimizations interact.

justifications.label: The heap spectrum and algorithm inheritance chain interact multiplicatively — Fibonacci heap's O(1) decrease-key cascades through Dijkstra to Yen's, demonstrating that data structure choices have transitive performance consequences across algorithm families

oracle-distributed-sql-synchronous-acces.text: Oracle Distributed SQL synchronously accesses and updates data distributed among multiple databases and includes distributed queries and distributed transactions.

oracle-nosql-composite-keys-major-minor.text: Oracle NoSQL supports composite keys with major and minor components analogous to file-system directory paths.

order-book-bid-ask-spread.text: The bid-ask spread is the difference between the highest bid and the lowest ask price (not averages or midpoints), serving as a key measure of liquidity and transaction cost

order-book-continuous-price-discovery.text: The order book supports continuous price discovery through the bid-ask spread, where the top of book (highest bid and lowest ask) represents the best available prices and signals prevailing market conditions; the matching engine reads this structure and pairs compatible orders for execution when buy and sell prices become compatible.

justifications.label: Spread defines the price uncertainty band; top-of-book narrows it; matching engine resolves it

order-book-crossed-book-abnormal.text: A crossed book is an abnormal state where the highest bid equals or exceeds the lowest ask but orders remain unmatched in the open book

order-book-dark-pool.text: A dark pool is a trading venue that uses an order book but obscures party identification from other participants

order-book-depth-chart-visualization.text: An order book depth chart visualizes price on the x-axis and cumulative order depth on the y-axis, with bids on the left and asks on the right.

order-book-depth-fixed-or-unlimited.text: Book depth is the number of price levels available and may be fixed, with orders beyond the depth rejected, or unlimited.

order-book-entry-minimum-fields.text: Each entry in an order book must contain at minimum: party identification, quantity, and price for the financial instrument

order-book-maintained-by-trading-venue.text: An order book is maintained by a trading venue such as a stock exchange and lists outstanding buy and sell orders for a particular financial instrument.

order-book-matching-engine-relationship.text: A matching engine reads the order book and pairs compatible buy and sell orders for execution; the order book is the data structure while the matching engine is the algorithm

order-book-multi-specialist-extension-me.text: Mertens' 2003 multi-specialist book extension allows order matching across specialists, with bids and offers expressed as linear functions of other traded items.

order-book-price-level.text: A price level is a group of orders sharing the same price; an incoming order at that price can potentially be matched against all orders on that level.

order-book-reliable-continuous-price-dis.text: The order book provides reliable continuous price discovery through FIFO matching at the best available prices, where the bid-ask spread and top-of-book converge on fair market value through the matching engine's execution of compatible orders.

justifications.label: Price discovery assumes a well-ordered book — a crossed book (bid ≥ ask with unmatched orders) breaks the mechanism

order-book-top-of-book-definition.text: The top of the book is defined as the highest bid price and the lowest ask price, representing the best available prices and signaling the prevalent market

order-matching-fifo-price-then-time.text: The Price/Time (FIFO) order matching algorithm prioritizes orders first by best price, then by arrival time

order-matching-operates-with-settlement-.text: Order matching systems operate within an electronic trading ecosystem that includes settlement systems and central securities depositories.

order-matching-pro-rata-proportional-fil.text: The Pro-Rata order matching algorithm distributes fills proportionally to order size at the best price level, incentivizing large limit orders

order-matching-replaced-open-outcry-earl.text: Order matching systems replaced and supplemented open outcry trading starting in the early 1980s.

order-matching-system-core-electronic-ex.text: An order matching system is an electronic system that matches buy and sell orders and is the core component of all electronic exchanges.

oriented-graph-at-most-one-direction.text: An oriented graph is a directed graph where at most one of (x, y) and (y, x) exists.

oso-order-one-sends-other.text: In a One Sends Other (OSO) order pair, execution of the primary order triggers submission of the dependent order.

ospf-isis-use-dijkstra-derived-shortest-.text: OSPF and IS-IS network routing protocols use shortest-path algorithms derived from Dijkstra's algorithm.

overbooking-relies-on-statistical-no-sho.text: Overbooking relies on statistical no-show rates to maximize utilization of available capacity.

overbooking-voluntary-before-involuntary.text: Airlines must seek volunteers before involuntarily denying boarding, required by both EU Regulation 261/2004 and US CFR Title 14 Part 250

overselling-deliberate-sale-above-supply.text: Overselling (overbooking) is the deliberate sale of a volatile good or service in excess of actual supply, based on the expectation that some buyers will cancel or not consume their entitlement.

oversubscription-ratio-formula.text: Oversubscription ratio equals (advertised bandwidth per user × number of users) divided by total shared bandwidth; e.g., (7 Mbit/s × 500) / 38 Mbit/s = 92:1

oversubscription-vs-overselling-distinct.text: Oversubscription is acceptable when it does not significantly degrade performance; overselling implies the ratio has crossed a threshold where users are materially impacted

p2pe-prevents-cleartext-card-data-exposu.text: Point-to-Point Encryption (P2PE) encrypts cardholder data so clear-text payment information is never accessible within the merchant's system, even during a breach

pacelc-extends-cap-latency-consistency-t.text: PACELC extends CAP: during a Partition choose Availability or Consistency; Else (no partition) choose Latency or Consistency.

pacioli-father-of-accounting-1494.text: Luca Pacioli published the first detailed description of double-entry bookkeeping in 1494 in Summa de arithmetica and is called the father of accounting; the earliest known European double-entry records are from the Farolfi ledger of 1299-1300.

panel-data-vs-time-series.text: A time series is a one-dimensional case of panel data; panel data requires both a time field and an additional identifier (e.g., stock symbol, country code)

parallel-shared-memory-vs-distributed-me.text: Parallel systems use shared memory for coordination, while distributed systems use private memory with message passing.

partial-failure-does-not-fail-whole-syst.text: In a distributed system, the partial failure principle means when one component fails, the entire system does not fail, distinguishing distributed systems from monolithic architectures.

partial-thread-safety-requires-applicati.text: Libraries may offer partial thread safety such as safe concurrent reads but unsafe concurrent writes, and applications must use them consistently with documented guarantees.

partition-binding-forces-approximate-cro.text: Kafka's partition-bound stateful processing creates an architectural pressure toward probabilistic sketches for cross-partition analytics: since RocksDB/LSM-backed state is confined to individual partitions, analytics spanning partition boundaries benefit from approximate mergeable structures (HLL for cardinality, Count-Min/Count Sketch for frequency) that can combine results without coordination, making probabilistic sketches a natural architectural complement to partition-local exact state rather than merely a convenience.

justifications.label: Partition binding constrains where exact state can live; the stream analytics dual requirement identifies what fills the gap — combining them reveals the causal mechanism (partition boundary) that makes sketches mandatory

partition-can-be-intentional-or-failure-.text: Network partitions can be created intentionally for optimization or caused by failure of network devices such as switches or routers.

partition-tolerance-affects-consistency-.text: Partition tolerance directly affects whether a system can maintain strong consistency or must fall back to eventual consistency.

partition-tolerance-continues-processing.text: Partition tolerance is the ability of a system to continue processing data even when a network partition causes communication errors between subsystems.

password-hashing-requires-kdf-not-sha.text: Standard cryptographic hashes (SHA family) are too fast for password storage; key derivation functions like PBKDF2, scrypt, or Argon2 with key stretching should be used instead

password-salt-prevents-rainbow-tables.text: A salt is a large random non-secret value hashed with passwords to prevent precomputed table attacks (rainbow tables)

patricia-is-binary-radix-tree.text: PATRICIA is a radix tree with radix 2 (binary), where each node stores the distinguishing bit position; invented by Donald R. Morrison in 1968

patricia-tree-compressed-binary-trie-wit.text: A Patricia tree is a compressed binary trie that uses binary encoding of keys and skip numbers to avoid traversing empty subtrees.

payment-front-end-vs-back-end-processor.text: Front-end payment processors handle authorization and settlement to merchant banks via card associations; back-end processors accept settlements and move funds from issuing bank to merchant bank

payment-network-chain-merchant-to-bank.text: The payment network architecture chain is: merchant → PoS SaaS → aggregator → credit card network → bank; small merchants cannot connect directly to aggregators or card networks due to low transaction volume

payment-processor-enables-merchant-custo.text: A payment processor is a system that enables financial transactions between merchants and customers across channels such as credit cards, debit cards, and bank accounts.

payment-processor-transaction-flow-inclu.text: In the payment transaction flow, the processor forwards card details to the issuing bank or card association for verification and runs anti-fraud checks before returning approval or denial via the payment gateway.

pbft-castro-liskov-1999-practical-bft.text: PBFT (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance) by Castro and Liskov (1999) was the breakthrough algorithm enabling high-throughput BFT with thousands of requests/sec.

peer-to-peer-architecture-no-special-ser.text: Peer-to-peer architecture has no special server machines; all peers serve as both client and server, as in BitTorrent and Bitcoin.

peg-order-tracks-reference-price.text: A peg order automatically tracks a reference price such as the best bid, best offer, or midpoint.

penny-jumping-front-running-mechanism.text: Penny jumping is a form of front-running where a trader places an order one tick ahead of a large visible limit order, risking only one tick of loss while capturing unlimited upside

perfect-hash-function-static-keys-only.text: A perfect hash function maps a known static key set with zero collisions but is computationally infeasible to find for large or dynamic key sets.

persist-then-acknowledge-validated-from-.text: The persist-then-acknowledge reliability pattern is demonstrated across a wide range of event processing frequencies — from email's retry windows measured in days to financial exchange order matching at extreme high-frequency scales — suggesting it functions as a frequency-resilient reliability primitive, though the evidence draws from two points on the spectrum rather than comprehensive coverage across it.

justifications.label: Reliability pattern holds from the slowest (email) to the fastest (exchange) event domains

persistence-and-distribution-compensatio.text: Sequential append-only persistence (converging along temporal and spatial axes from email through Kafka to S3) and the distribution-plus-compensation pattern (layer-invariant across content and data) together address two major orthogonal concerns in distributed systems — persistence determines HOW data is durably recorded while distribution-plus-compensation determines WHERE it is placed and HOW consistency is restored — suggesting these two patterns jointly cover significant architectural ground, though the evidence does not establish that they constitute the complete meta-architecture.

justifications.label: Persistence and distribution-compensation are the two orthogonal meta-architectural axes governing all distributed designs

pert-critical-path-is-longest-path.text: In PERT/critical path scheduling, vertices are milestones, edges are tasks with time estimates, and the longest path is the critical path controlling project duration.

pessimistic-locking-requires-persistent-.text: Pessimistic locking requires a persistent database connection and is not suitable for web applications.

pessimistic-vs-optimistic-locking.text: Pessimistic locking acquires exclusive lock on read (best for high-contention, short-hold); optimistic locking allows concurrent reads and checks for changes on write (best for low-contention, disconnected/web scenarios)

phantom-deadlocks-distributed-false-posi.text: Phantom deadlocks are false positives in distributed deadlock detection caused by communication delays, where the detected deadlock no longer exists at detection time

pipe-blocking-io-prevents-deadlock.text: Read and write calls on Unix pipes are blocking — a writer suspends when the buffer is full, a reader suspends when empty — and this cannot cause deadlock because the OS will always service at least one side

pipe-buffers-exist-at-kernel-and-user-le.text: Pipe buffers exist at both the kernel level (automatic, small) and user level (the buffer command, configurable size).

pipeline-buffering-handles-rate-differen.text: Buffering is typically provided between consecutive pipeline elements to handle rate differences between producer and consumer.

pipeline-return-channel-allows-reverse-c.text: A pipeline return channel (backchannel) allows limited reverse communication, such as the lexer hack.

pipes-and-filters-design-pattern.text: The software pipeline pattern is also known as the pipes and filters design pattern and is analogous to physical plumbing and function composition.

pipes-filters-monolithic-pattern-tradeof.text: The pipes and filters design pattern is classified as a monolithic architecture style, offering simplicity and low cost but lacking elasticity, fault tolerance, and scalability

plausible-clocks-constant-size-sacrifice.text: Plausible clocks (1999) are a constant-size alternative to vector clocks that sacrifices precision and may total-order concurrent events.

plru-flips-pointers-away-from-accessed-i.text: PLRU on access flips the 1-bit pointers along the path away from the accessed item to find an eviction candidate.

plru-one-bit-per-item-binary-tree.text: Pseudo-LRU (PLRU) approximates LRU using a binary tree structure requiring only 1 bit per cache item, making it practical for CPU caches with high associativity

pnr-is-core-booking-record-managed-by-cr.text: A Passenger Name Record (PNR) is the core data record created and managed by a CRS for each booking.

point-quadtree-average-olog-n-worst-line.text: A point quadtree operates in O(log n) average time but has worst-case linear height sensitive to insertion order.

point-quadtree-centers-subdivision-on-in.text: A point quadtree centers subdivision on inserted points, producing cells that are rectangular but not necessarily square.

point-quadtree-superseded-by-kd-trees.text: Point quadtrees have been largely superseded by k-d trees for generalized binary search on point data

poison-message-repeated-consumer-failure.text: A poison message repeatedly causes consumer failure and is closely related to the DLQ max-receive-count routing reason.

polyphase-filter-decomposes-fir-into-m-s.text: Polyphase decomposition splits a length-K FIR filter into M sub-filters (phases), each operating on a demultiplexed stream of the input, enabling parallel and multi-processor implementations of decimation

polytree-is-oriented-undirected-tree.text: A polytree is a multitree formed by orienting the edges of an undirected tree.

positional-indexing-required-for-proximi.text: Positional indexing (storing word positions within documents, not just term presence) is required at the indexing layer to support proximity queries

posix-open-flock-and-pthreads-provide-os.text: OS-level atomicity primitives include POSIX open(2) and flock(2) for atomic file open/lock and POSIX Threads for synchronization.

postgresql-wal-parameters-include-wal-le.text: PostgreSQL WAL is configured via parameters such as `wal_level`, `checkpoint_timeout`, and `max_wal_size`.

power-of-two-choices-load-balancing.text: Power of two choices: pick two servers randomly, choose the less loaded one — a simple algorithm with surprisingly good distribution properties

powershell-object-pipelines-not-text.text: PowerShell pipelines pass structured .NET objects between stages, not byte/text streams like Unix pipes

prefix-sum-optimal-distribution-log-n.text: When task sizes are known and divisible, prefix sum algorithms give optimal load distribution in O(log n) time

presence-is-fundamental-im-component.text: Presence (online status tracking) is a fundamental IM system component requiring its own protocol support, not just a UI feature

presumed-commit-optimization-assumes-com.text: Presumed commit optimization in 2PC assumes commit unless abort evidence is found during recovery.

price-elasticity-high-vs-low-sensitivity.text: High-elasticity products are price-sensitive, while low-elasticity products are less price-sensitive and typically more valued by consumers.

prim-structurally-similar-to-dijkstra-bu.text: Prim's algorithm is structurally similar to Dijkstra's algorithm as a greedy priority-queue algorithm but solves minimum spanning tree rather than shortest paths, and Dijkstra rediscovered Prim's algorithm.

primary-backup-single-leader-handles-all.text: In primary-backup (single-leader) replication, one designated leader handles all writes while replicas serve reads.

priority-inversion-mitigation.text: Priority inversion occurs when a low-priority thread holding a lock blocks high-priority threads; it is mitigated by priority inheritance or the priority ceiling protocol

priority-inversion-related-to-mutex-usag.text: Priority inversion is a concurrency hazard related to mutex usage.

priority-r-tree-worst-case-optimal.text: The Priority R-tree is the only R-tree variant with worst-case optimal query performance, but it is impractical

probabilistic-analytics-complete-unless-.text: The complete probabilistic analytics layer for partition-bound stream processing — membership, cardinality, and frequency estimation all independently mergeable across partitions — holds only when the underlying sketches remain linearly combinable, which conservative update optimization in Count-Min Sketch breaks.

justifications.label: Cross-partition mergeability is the prerequisite for distributed analytics completeness — conservative update breaks the frequency estimation link in the chain

probabilistic-efficiency-through-analyti.text: Probabilistic data structures achieve practical efficiency through analytically derivable optimal configurations rather than empirical tuning — Bloom filters' closed-form space model (k = (m/n)·ln(2) yielding 9.6 bits/element at 1% FP) and HyperLogLog's three-stage estimation pipeline (harmonic mean + bias correction + small-range correction yielding 1.04/√m relative error) both reduce deployment to parameter selection from proven formulas.

justifications.label: Both Bloom and HLL have closed-form optimal configurations derivable from first principles rather than empirical search

probabilistic-estimation-analytically-pr.text: All three major probabilistic query families achieve efficiency through analytically principled estimation pipelines rather than empirical tuning — membership (Bloom filter's closed-form k = (m/n)·ln(2) optimal hash count), cardinality (HyperLogLog's harmonic-mean bias-corrected pipeline), and frequency estimation (Count Sketch's linear projection via pairwise-independent hashing with non-linear median reconstruction) — establishing analytic derivability as a defining characteristic of the entire probabilistic data structure design space.

justifications.label: All three probabilistic query families share analytically principled pipelines, extending from Bloom/HLL to Count Sketch

probabilistic-query-taxonomy-three-ortho.text: The probabilistic data structure landscape includes at least three query types — membership (Bloom/quotient filters), cardinality (HyperLogLog), and frequency (Count-Min/Count Sketch) — each addressing a distinct aggregate question with sublinear space by trading exactness for compressed statistical summaries. Quotient filters and HyperLogLog support mergeability, enabling distributed operation, though the antecedents do not establish that all three families are independently mergeable or that these three types are exhaustive or strictly orthogonal.

justifications.label: Three orthogonal probabilistic query types form a complete sublinear-space analytics taxonomy

probabilistic-sketches-algebraically-mer.text: Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min sketches are all algebraically mergeable (bitwise OR, element-wise max, and element-wise add respectively), enabling a distributed computation pattern where partial sketches are combined without access to original data.

justifications.label: Mergeability is the shared property that makes probabilistic data structures practical in distributed systems — each uses a different algebraic operation but all support combine-without-replay

probabilistic-streaming-lineage-morris-t.text: The probabilistic streaming algorithm lineage traces from Morris's approximate counting (1977) through Flajolet's analysis (1980s) to modern sketches (HyperLogLog 2007, Count-Min, Count Sketch), sharing a common design principle: trading exactness for exponential space reduction by storing compressed statistical summaries rather than exact values.

justifications.label: Morris → Flajolet → HLL traces a direct intellectual lineage where each generation applies the same space-for-accuracy tradeoff at increasing sophistication

probabilistic-structures-analytically-pr.text: Probabilistic data structures combine two notable properties — analytically derivable optimal configurations (closed-form space models for Bloom filters, bias-corrected estimation pipelines for HyperLogLog, pairwise-independent projection with median reconstruction for Count Sketch) and broad applicability as scale compensation mechanisms across distributed systems (infrastructure domains like crawler deduplication and processing domains like partition-bound stream analytics) — making analytic derivability a defining characteristic of the design space and positioning these structures as a primary class where mathematical precision in design translates to practical scalability.

justifications.label: Analytic precision in design and universal scale compensation are jointly unique to probabilistic structures

probabilistic-structures-combine-analyti.text: Probabilistic data structures achieve practical scale compensation through analytically derivable optimal configurations — the closed-form mathematical models (Bloom's k=(m/n)·ln(2), HLL's 1.04/√m) eliminate empirical tuning, and these optimally-configured structures serve as the universal compensation mechanism for scaling tradeoffs across both infrastructure (crawler deduplication) and processing (partition-bound stream analytics) domains.

justifications.label: Analytic optimality (closed-form parameterization) makes probabilistic structures practical at scale; universal compensation role makes them mandatory

probabilistic-structures-universal-scale.text: Probabilistic data structures serve as a primary compensation mechanism for scaling tradeoffs in distributed systems — AMQ structures (Bloom and quotient filters) address LSM storage read amplification with zero-false-negative guarantees, while algebraically mergeable sketches (HLL, Count-Min, Count Sketch) enable coordination-free approximate analytics for distributed stream processing.

justifications.label: Two independent probabilistic compensation strategies (storage reads via AMQ, stream analytics via mergeable sketches) reveal a universal pattern: probabilistic structures compensate wherever exact computation doesn't scale

probabilistic-taxonomy-completes-partiti.text: The three orthogonal probabilistic query types (membership via Bloom/quotient filters, cardinality via HyperLogLog, frequency via Count-Min/Count Sketch) align naturally with cross-partition analytics needs created by partition-bound stateful processing — each mergeable sketch type addresses a category of information that is difficult to obtain across partition boundaries, collectively providing an approximate analytics layer that complements what exact per-partition state can offer.

justifications.label: The probabilistic taxonomy (depth-2) identifies three query types; partition binding (depth-4) creates the architectural pressure for approximation — the precise mapping of query types to partition-boundary information loss is emergent

processes-unknown-happened-before-withou.text: Processes have no knowledge of the happened-before relation unless they use a logical clock.

prometheus-four-metric-types.text: Prometheus supports four metric types: Counter (monotonically increasing), Gauge (arbitrary up/down), Histogram (server-side bucketed observations), and Summary (client-side quantile calculation)

prometheus-multidimensional-data-model-l.text: Prometheus metrics are identified by a name plus arbitrary key-value label pairs (e.g., instance, job, HTTP method, status code), enabling flexible slicing and querying.

prometheus-open-source-monitoring-alerti.text: Prometheus is an open-source monitoring and alerting toolkit that records metrics in a time-series database.

prometheus-pull-model-scrapes-targets.text: Prometheus uses a pull-based collection model where the server periodically scrapes configured targets via HTTP, as opposed to push-based systems like StatsD

prometheus-requires-grafana-for-dashboar.text: Prometheus includes only a basic expression browser and does not provide a full dashboard system; Grafana is the standard pairing for production dashboards

prometheus-second-cncf-project-graduated.text: Prometheus was the second CNCF-hosted project after Kubernetes (accepted May 2016, graduated August 2018), originated at SoundCloud in 2012 inspired by Google's Borgmon

prometheus-service-discovery-locates-scr.text: Prometheus service discovery automatically locates scrape targets in dynamic environments such as containerized or cloud-native infrastructure.

prometheus-storage-wal-inverted-index-co.text: Prometheus local storage uses WAL for crash durability, an inverted index for label-based queries, and background compaction to merge blocks; default retention is weeks, not months

prometheus-white-box-monitoring-exporter.text: Prometheus favors white-box monitoring, where applications expose internal metrics via exporters rather than external probing.

prometheus-written-in-go-apache-2.text: Prometheus is written in Go and licensed under Apache 2.0.

promql-supports-instant-range-vectors-an.text: PromQL is Prometheus's native query language and supports instant vectors, range vectors, and functions such as rate().

proprietary-im-protocols-create-walled-g.text: Most major IM networks use proprietary protocols, creating walled gardens, while open standards such as XMPP and SIP/SIMPLE have attempted interoperability.

proximity-search-combats-spamdexing.text: Proximity search penalizes keyword-stuffed pages because scattered terms won't appear near each other, making it an anti-spamdexing technique

proximity-search-linguistic-assumption-p.text: Proximity search relies on the linguistic assumption that words appearing near each other in a document are more likely to be semantically related because authors cluster related ideas into sentences and paragraphs.

proximity-search-measures-distance-betwe.text: Proximity search finds documents where search terms occur within a specified distance of each other, measured in intermediate words or characters

proximity-search-ordered-vs-unordered.text: Proximity search has two key dimensions: distance (how many words apart) and order (whether terms must appear in query order)

proximity-search-reduces-recall-increase.text: Proximity constraints reduce recall but increase precision compared to basic keyword search

pss-three-components.text: A Passenger Service System (PSS) encompasses three components: reservations, inventory management, and departure control.

ptp-sub-microsecond-lan-master-slave.text: PTP (IEEE 1588) achieves sub-microsecond accuracy over LANs using a master/slave architecture

pub-sub-one-to-many-point-to-point-one-t.text: Publish/subscribe is a one-to-many delivery pattern, while point-to-point is a one-to-one delivery pattern.

pubsub-distinct-from-observer-pattern.text: Pub/sub is distinct from the observer pattern: pub/sub emphasizes distributed, broker-mediated, asynchronous communication while observer handles in-process events

pubsub-first-described-isis-toolkit-1987.text: The publish-subscribe pattern was first described publicly in the Isis Toolkit at SOSP '87 (Birman & Joseph, 1987)

pubsub-highest-decoupling-among-messagin.text: Pub/sub provides the highest level of decoupling among messaging patterns compared to RPC and point-to-point

pubsub-implemented-by-kafka-mqtt-jms-and.text: Apache Kafka, MQTT, JMS, and DDS are frameworks or protocols that implement publish-subscribe messaging.

pubsub-is-sibling-of-message-queue-parad.text: Pub/sub is a sibling of the message queue paradigm rather than a replacement; queues deliver to one consumer while pub/sub delivers to all matching subscribers.

pubsub-message-broker-routes-messages-fr.text: In publish-subscribe, a message broker or event bus receives messages from publishers and routes them to subscribers, optionally performing store-and-forward, priority queuing, or routing logic.

pubsub-no-inherent-delivery-guarantee.text: The publish-subscribe pattern does not inherently guarantee message delivery; additional design such as subscriber acknowledgment is needed for guaranteed delivery

pubsub-publishers-subscribers-decoupled.text: In publish-subscribe, publishers send messages categorized by topic without knowledge of subscribers, and subscribers register interest without knowledge of publishers, achieving spatial, temporal, and identity decoupling

pubsub-security-risk-includes-broker-mis.text: Pub/sub security risks include brokers being tricked into misdirecting messages and unauthorized publishers injecting bad data.

pubsub-subscription-registration-timing-.text: Pub/sub subscription registration can occur at build time via hardcoded handlers, at initialization time via XML config or metadata, or at runtime via dynamically added or removed subscriptions.

pubsub-three-filtering-types.text: Pub/sub supports three message filtering approaches: topic-based (named channels), content-based (attribute constraints), and hybrid (topic then content filters)

pubsub-topic-based-filtering-delivers-al.text: In topic-based publish-subscribe filtering, subscribers receive all messages published on the topics they have subscribed to.

purchase-ledger-alias-creditors-ledger.text: The purchase ledger is also called the creditors ledger.

purely-functional-languages-immutable-ob.text: In purely functional programming languages, all objects are immutable, making data structures inherently append-only.

push-clients-express-interest-via-publis.text: In push technology, clients typically express interest by subscribing to channels using the publish-subscribe pattern, and the server pushes updates to those channels automatically.

push-server-initiated-pull-client-initia.text: Push technology is server-initiated data delivery while pull technology is client-initiated requests; these are the two fundamental communication directions

push-simulated-by-polling-when-http-inbo.text: When security policies block incoming HTTP requests, push technology is sometimes simulated using polling techniques.

put-idempotent-sets-state-post-not-creat.text: PUT is idempotent because it sets a resource to a specific state (like variable assignment); POST is not because it creates new resources (like appending to a list)

python-file-is-module-and-package-direct.text: In Python, each file is a module and directories with __init__.py are packages that group modules.

python-immutable-types-int-str-tuple-fro.text: Python's built-in immutable types are int, str, tuple, and frozenset; frozen dataclasses and NamedTuples provide immutable custom classes

python-siphash-per-process-seed.text: Python uses SipHash with a per-process random seed, so hash values are deterministic within one execution but not stable across processes, which prevents hash-flooding DoS attacks.

quadratic-probing-reduces-primary-cluste.text: Quadratic probing resolves collisions by checking slots h+1 squared, h+2 squared, h+3 squared, and so on, and reduces primary clustering compared with linear probing.

quadtree-four-children-per-internal-node.text: A quadtree is a tree where each internal node has exactly four children (NW, NE, SW, SE), used to recursively partition 2D space; it is the 2D analog of octrees

quadtree-invented-finkel-bentley-1974.text: Quadtrees were invented by Raphael Finkel and J.L. Bentley in 1974

quasi-random-skip-list-levels-resist-adv.text: Quasi-random skip list level construction protects against adversaries deleting high-level nodes to degrade performance.

quorum-commit-abort-mutual-exclusion.text: The safety invariant Va + Vc > V ensures a distributed transaction cannot simultaneously commit and abort (mutual exclusion of outcomes)

quorum-enforces-one-copy-serializability.text: Quorum-based replica control enforces one-copy serializability, making replicated data behave as if only one copy exists

quorum-majority-partition-progress-minor.text: In a network partition, the majority partition can make progress under quorum systems while the minority partition cannot reach quorum.

quorum-minimum-votes-required-to-authori.text: A quorum is the minimum number of votes a distributed transaction must obtain to perform an operation.

quorum-read-write-overlap-formula.text: In quorum-based replica control, Vr + Vw > V guarantees a read quorum overlaps with any write quorum so reads always see the latest version

quorum-sizes-tunable-for-workload.text: Quorum sizes are tunable: low Vr + high Vw favors read-heavy workloads; high Vr + low Vw favors write-heavy workloads

quorum-tuning-implements-cap-spectrum.text: Quorum-based replication offers tunability within consistency-availability tradeoffs — the read-write overlap formula (Vr + Vw > V) provides a consistency guarantee by ensuring read and write quorums intersect, while adjustable quorum sizes allow shifting between read-optimized and write-optimized configurations. Sloppy quorums extend this by allowing writes to available nodes when designated replicas are down, trading strict consistency for availability during failures.

justifications.label: Strict quorum overlap guarantees consistency; tunable sizes implement the workload spectrum; sloppy quorum breaks the consistency guarantee for availability — a continuous CAP dial

quorum-two-primary-uses-replica-control-.text: Quorum-based techniques have two primary uses: replica control for managing concurrent access to replicated data and commit protocols for ensuring transaction atomicity during network partitions.

quorum-voting-requires-threshold-not-una.text: Quorum-based voting requires only a threshold of votes, not unanimous agreement from all sites.

quorum-write-conflict-avoidance-formula.text: The constraint Vw > V/2 prevents two concurrent writes to the same replicated data item (write-write conflict avoidance)

quotient-bloom-amq-design-space.text: Quotient filters and Bloom filters both guarantee zero false negatives but occupy different points in the AMQ design space: quotient filters preserve fingerprints enabling merging and resizing without original keys, while Bloom filters sacrifice this for simpler bitwise operations.

justifications.label: The no-false-negative guarantee is shared; the differentiator is whether the filter preserves enough information for structural operations beyond membership testing

quotient-filter-cluster-contiguous-runs-.text: A cluster in a quotient filter is a contiguous sequence of runs starting from a run whose first fingerprint occupies its canonical slot and terminating at an empty slot or the next cluster start.

quotient-filter-cluster-length-olog-m.text: In a quotient filter with uniform hashing, most runs are O(1) and all runs are highly likely O(log m) in the worst case, where m is the number of slots

quotient-filter-fingerprint-split.text: A quotient filter splits a p-bit hash fingerprint into a q-bit quotient (high-order bits, determines slot) and an r-bit remainder (low-order bits, stored in slot), with 2^q slots in the table
